The ads get clicks. The discovery call gets overlooked. I’d start with the promise on the page.

A leadership coach with a strong personal brand runs Meta ads to a landing page offering a "Free Discovery Call." The ads get clicks, but the booking rate is low. The landing page has a professional photo, a headline about "unlocking potential," and a long paragraph about the coach's credentials.
The headline describes the coach, not the client's problem.
The "Free Discovery Call" offer feels vague – the visitor doesn't know what will happen on the call.
The call-to-action is buried below a wall of text.
The page is focused on "who I am" instead of "what you get."
– name the specific problem the client solves (e.g., "Stop second-guessing your leadership decisions").
– "Free Discovery Call" → "30-Minute Leadership Audit" – a tangible, outcome-focused offer.
– put a clear, benefit-focused paragraph above the fold.
– "In this 30-minute session, we'll identify your leadership blindspots and map out a 90-day plan."
A/B test headline variation A vs. B. Test the "Leadership Audit" offer against the "Discovery Call" offer. Measure booking rate and show-up rate.
A creative agency team reviewing website wireframes
A long list of services leaves visitors with too many decisions. I’d build a focused entry point.
One services page tries to sell everything, while the next step feels generic.
Match the page to the service people need, with a clear audit offer and relevant proof.
Compare the focused page with the original. Track enquiries and cost per lead.

A small digital agency runs Google Ads to a "Services" page. The page lists everything they do – web design, SEO, content, branding, and social media – in one long block. Visitors land, scan, and leave. Leads are rare.
The page has no clear entry point – it tries to sell everything to everyone.
There's no "hook" – no reason for a visitor to say "this is for me."
The call-to-action ("Contact Us") is generic and offers no incentive.
– dedicated landing page for each service, or one page with a clear "pick your path" entry.
– "Free 30-Minute Audit for Service Businesses" – tangible and low-friction.
– name a specific audience pain point (e.g., "Stop getting lost in the noise – get seen by the right people").
– real logos, even if small, to build trust.
– "Contact Us" → "Book Your Free Audit" linked to a calendar.
Audit landing page vs. services page. Measure conversion rate (lead submissions) and cost per lead. Test different lead magnet offers (audit vs. consultation vs. checklist).
A renovation professional and homeowner reviewing plans
Turn interest into a real conversation.
A contact form alone gives homeowners little reason to act. I’d make the consultation feel useful and credible.
A generic quote request gives browsers and ready-to-buy visitors the same experience.
Show relevant project work, explain the process and offer a useful consultation.
Compare consultation bookings and the quality of project enquiries.

A local home renovation company runs Facebook ads to a "Contact Us" page. The page has a phone number, an email form, and a list of services (kitchens, bathrooms, extensions). The lead volume is low and inconsistent.
The page treats every visitor the same – no distinction between "browsers" and "ready-to-buy."
The offer ("Get a Quote") is generic – no reason to take action today.
No trust-building content – testimonials, before/after photos, or case studies are missing.
– "We've renovated 100+ homes – see what it could look like for yours."
– "Get a Quote" → "Book a Free Consultation – We'll walk your project with you."
– simple portfolio with before/after images to build credibility.
– separate page for each major service (kitchens, bathrooms, extensions) with targeted messaging.
Test the "Book a Consultation" landing page against the existing "Contact Us" page. Measure consultation bookings and lead quality (number of actual project enquiries vs. general enquiries).
